subject: Polity
description: 10th Schedule, 52nd Amendment, 91st Amendment, grounds for disqualification, Speaker's role

questions.stem: The Anti-Defection law was added to the Constitution by which Constitutional Amendment?

options.option_text: 44th Amendment, in 1978 after the Emergency
52nd Amendment, in 1985 by the Rajiv Gandhi government
73rd Amendment, in 1992 for panchayati raj reforms
91st Amendment, in 2003 strengthening the existing rules

questions.explanation: 52nd Amendment, 1985 — added the TENTH SCHEDULE to the Constitution. Aim: prevent 'aaya ram gaya ram' political defections that had destabilised governments since the 1960s. The 91st Amendment (2003) significantly strengthened the law — abolished the 'split' provision (1/3 defection allowed) and barred defectors from holding ministerial / paid offices for the rest of the term. Distractor 1 = 44th amendment was about restoring rights changed during Emergency. Distractor 3 = 73rd was about panchayats. Distractor 4 = 91st only AMENDED an existing law, didn't create it.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under the 10th Schedule, a member of Parliament can be DISQUALIFIED for defection on which ground?

options.option_text: Voting against the Prime Minister's personal preference
Voluntarily giving up party membership or defying party whip
Switching constituencies between two general elections
Failing to attend the parliamentary session for one whole month

questions.explanation: 10th Schedule grounds for disqualification: (a) voluntarily giving up membership of the party that elected the member; (b) voting / abstaining contrary to the party whip's direction (UNLESS prior permission obtained or condoned within 15 days); (c) for an INDEPENDENT member — joining any party after election; (d) for a NOMINATED member — joining a party 6 months after taking the seat. Distractor 1 — there's no PM-vote rule. Distractor 3 — constituency switching is allowed before election. Distractor 4 — absenteeism is not a defection ground (though prolonged absence can lead to vacancy under separate Article 101).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Decisions on defection cases under the 10th Schedule are made by:

options.option_text: The Election Commission of India after due investigation
The presiding officer (Speaker / Chairman) of the House concerned
The President of India based on a parliamentary motion
A committee of three retired Supreme Court judges

questions.explanation: Speaker (Lok Sabha) / Chairman (Rajya Sabha) decides disqualification cases under the 10th Schedule. CRITICISM — Speaker often elected from the ruling party; perceived bias. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1993) — SC held Speaker's decisions are JUSTICIABLE (subject to judicial review), but NOT before the decision is made. Recent SC rulings (2020 — Manipur case) have suggested Parliament consider an INDEPENDENT TRIBUNAL for defection cases instead of the Speaker. Distractor 1 — ECI handles election-related disqualifications under Articles 102 and 191, not defection (which is purely 10th Schedule). Distractor 3 — President doesn't directly decide. Distractor 4 — invented.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Which exception EXISTS in the 10th Schedule that allows party-membership change WITHOUT triggering disqualification?

options.option_text: Defection by 1/3 of the legislative party (the 'split' exception)
Merger with another party if 2/3 of the legislative party agree
Defection if the leader of the legislative party also defects
Defection during a no-confidence motion in the House

questions.explanation: EXCEPTIONS in 10th Schedule (post-91st Amendment, 2003): (1) MERGER — if 2/3 (not just 1/3) of the legislative party members agree to MERGE the party with another, NO disqualification. The 'two-thirds' rule effectively ended the easier 'split' exception. (2) Speaker / Chairman / Deputy Speaker — leaving original party for impartiality reasons doesn't disqualify; rejoining after vacating the chair also doesn't. Distractor 1 — the 1/3 'split' exception was REMOVED by 91st Amendment. Distractors 3, 4 are invented.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: The 91st Amendment (2003) ALSO imposed which limit on the size of the Council of Ministers?

options.option_text: Limited the Council to a maximum of 25 ministers
Capped it at 15% of the strength of the Lok Sabha
Required the Council to mirror the ruling alliance's composition
Mandated a minimum of 33% women in the cabinet

questions.explanation: 91st Amendment, 2003 — added Article 75(1A) and 164(1A): the total number of ministers (including PM/CM) shall not exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha (or state legislative assembly). For smaller states (assembly under 40 members), the ceiling is 12 ministers. Aim: end the 'jumbo cabinets' that emerged in coalition governments where dozens of MPs were rewarded with ministerial posts. Distractor 1 — no fixed-number cap. Distractor 3 — no such mirror requirement. Distractor 4 — no women-quota requirement (separate Women's Reservation Act now exists for legislatures, not cabinet).
questions.subject: Polity

options.option_text: Only members of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha at the Centre
MPs plus members of state legislative assemblies and councils
Cabinet ministers and ministers of state at the Centre alone
Local body members in panchayats and city municipalities

questions.explanation: 10th Schedule applies to: Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha + State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabha) + State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad, in 6 states). Disqualification under Schedule 10 leads to LOSS OF SEAT in the legislature. Distractor 1 misses state legislatures. Distractor 3 — applies to ALL legislators, not just ministers. Distractor 4 — local bodies are governed by separate state laws on defection (some states have local-body anti-defection rules but they are NOT under the 10th Schedule).
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: A common criticism of the Anti-Defection law is that it:

options.option_text: Encourages frequent toppling of state governments unfairly
Curtails legitimate dissent within a party by binding to whip
Costs the exchequer too much in tribunal-related fees
Makes individual MPs more independent of their parties

questions.explanation: Major criticisms: (1) Stifles INDEPENDENT JUDGMENT — MPs/MLAs must vote with the whip on every party-line vote, even if they disagree on conscience; reduces deliberative quality of legislation. (2) SPEAKER'S BIAS — Speaker is from ruling party, may delay or favour decisions politically. (3) DELAYED DECISIONS — Karnataka 2019, Maharashtra 2022 cases dragged on for months / years. (4) Doesn't prevent 'horse trading' done before sworn-in via 'resign-and-rejoin' (Karnataka, MP recent cases). Calls to reform: limit whip to crucial votes (no-confidence, money bills); independent tribunal in place of Speaker. Distractor 1 — opposite of intended/observed. Distractor 4 — opposite (it makes MPs MORE bound to parties).
